questions.prompt: You repeatedly tune prompts to fix the held-out set. What happens to its role?

options.label: Its independence improves because the score rises.
It becomes equivalent to a production randomized trial.
It becomes development evidence; use fresh held-out cases for the next unbiased check.

questions.explanation: Repeated tuning leaks evaluation feedback into development. A higher fitted score is not independent evidence, and offline tuning is not a production trial.

questions.prompt: A candidate gets 90/100 correct but fails all ten warranty exceptions. What should the report show?

options.label: 100%, after removing exceptions from the denominator post hoc.
The overall rate, the failed exception slice, counts and severity.
Only 90%, because subgroup outcomes would complicate the story.

questions.explanation: Critical slices can determine rollout even when averages look good. Hiding or retroactively excluding failures misrepresents the task population.

questions.prompt: How can you compare two prompt versions more fairly offline?

options.label: Use the same cases and rubric, record versions, and inspect paired wins and losses.
Give the new version only easy questions and compare averages.
Change corpus, model and task mix without recording them.

questions.explanation: Matched cases make differences interpretable. Different difficulty and undocumented simultaneous changes confound the comparison.

questions.prompt: Which evidence is needed to reproduce an evaluation result?

options.label: Only a screenshot of the final percentage.
Only the provider name with no dataset or prompt identity.
Inputs, rubric, relevant configuration versions and per-case judgments.

questions.explanation: Reproduction needs the tested system and judgments, not just its headline score. Provider identity alone leaves major variables unspecified.
